summary: The dispatch-time gate is correctly wired into task-gateway.py's cmd_start() immediately after tight_task_validation.py and before veridian-task.py create -- the one real chokepoint before a worker is spawned -- and the new tests pass for the cases they cover, so the plumbing itself is sound. However the detection logic has several concrete bypasses that reproduce the exact class of risk the cited incident represents: the PRE-APPROVED-LIVE-DDL citation is never checked against any real approval record (OWNER_DECISIONS_NEEDED yaml, decision log, etc.) -- it only has to avoid a short placeholder denylist, so the same prompt-authoring process that caused the original incident can defeat this gate by writing any freeform non-placeholder string after the marker; the DDL keyword regexes require exact adjacency (CREATE TABLE, CREATE INDEX, ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE, TRUNCATE) and miss common variants entirely undetected (CREATE UNIQUE INDEX, DROP INDEX/VIEW/SCHEMA/FUNCTION, CREATE/DROP POLICY for RLS, RENAME TABLE, GRANT/REVOKE); and tool-name detection only matches the literal string apply_migration, so a prompt instructing a worker to use another DDL-capable Supabase MCP tool (e.g. execute_sql) without spelling out a matched keyword sails through untouched. Because this is a static text scan of the prompt file rather than runtime tool-call interception, a prompt phrased in prose ("reconcile the schema drift using whatever Supabase tools are necessary") without literal DDL keywords bypasses the gate entirely while the worker can still invoke DDL-capable tools at execution time. The change is additive/isolated and does not itself introduce a new vulnerability, but PROTOCOL_OWNER_AI.yaml now permanently records this incident class as 'Fixed,' which overstates what was actually closed and risks a future Superboss session treating the DDL-authorization risk as resolved when it is only partially mitigated.
issues: PRE-APPROVED-LIVE-DDL citation is accepted as valid whenever it is merely non-empty and not on a short placeholder denylist (find_pre_approval in scripts/ddl_authorization_check.py) -- there is no cross-check against any real Owner-approval record, so any prompt author can self-approve with an arbitrary string like 'approved' or 'see chat', defeating the exact self-authorization failure mode the incident exposed.

DDL keyword regexes require exact phrase adjacency and miss common real-world DDL variants entirely: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX, DROP INDEX, DROP VIEW/SCHEMA/FUNCTION, CREATE/DROP POLICY (RLS policy DDL -- explicitly security-sensitive per this repo's own tier2 rules), RENAME TABLE, and GRANT/REVOKE all pass through undetected.

Tool-name detection only matches the literal string 'apply_migration'; other DDL-capable Supabase MCP tools (e.g. execute_sql) are not covered, so a prompt directing a worker to use them for schema changes is not flagged even when it also fails to use a matched keyword.

The gate is a static text scan of the prompt file at dispatch time, not runtime tool-call interception -- a prose-only prompt that doesn't spell out literal SQL/tool names bypasses the gate while the worker retains the ability to invoke DDL-capable tools at execution time; this closes the literal wording of the one cited incident but not the general class of risk.

PROTOCOL_OWNER_AI.yaml's new A15 article states the gap is 'Fixed by scripts/ddl_authorization_check.py' -- given the above gaps this is an overstatement that should be softened to 'partially mitigated' so future sessions don't treat dispatch-time DDL risk as fully resolved.
